svg.title: Roman Britain (Britannia): Aqueducts, Baths & Stone Sewers (AD 43–410)
svg.desc: KS3 Year 7 historical GIS atlas map of Roman Britain (AD 43–410) on an unpartitioned British Isles base without modern England, Wales, Scotland, or Northern Ireland borders, land-clipping Roman Britannia south of Hadrian’s Wall against unconquered Caledonia in the north, plotting Watling Street, the Fosse Way, and Ermine Street, and highlighting Londinium, Aquae Sulis (Bath), Lindum (Lincoln) and Durnovaria (Dorchester) aqueducts, and Eboracum (York) and Housesteads stone latrines.

g.text: Fresh hill spring water piped into Roman towns

text.tspan: Stone sewers & communal sponge-stick soldier latrines
Gravity-fed aqueducts pipe hill spring water to towns
Capital with timber & lead pipes, bathhouses & drains
Sacred hot-spring thermae & lead-lined Great Bath

svg.text: KS3 HISTORY • YEAR 7 ENQUIRY: WATER, SANITATION & PUBLIC HEALTH
Roman Britain (Britannia): Aqueducts, Baths & Stone Sewers (AD 43–410)
After invading in AD 43, Roman engineers built gravity-fed stone aqueducts, heated bathhouses (thermae), and flushing drains.
Yet shared sponge sticks, uncleaned bathwater, and toxic lead pipes still spread parasites—and water systems collapsed after AD 410.
